author: high
claim: If a finite undirected graph is bipartite, then it contains no cycle of odd length.
evidence: Let V(G)=A∪B be a bipartition, so every edge has one endpoint in A and one in B. Along any cycle, successive vertices therefore alternate between A and B. Returning to the starting vertex requires an even number of edge traversals, so every cycle has even length.

links.statement: If G is bipartite, every cycle in G has even length.

glossary.G: the finite undirected graph in the theorem
glossary.A: one vertex class in a bipartition
glossary.B: the other vertex class in a bipartition
glossary.T: a spanning tree of a connected component of G
glossary.r: a chosen root vertex of T
glossary.d_T(r,v): the number of edges on the unique path in T from r to v

author: high
claim: If a finite undirected graph contains no cycle of odd length, then parity of depth in a rooted spanning tree of each component gives a bipartition.
evidence: For each connected component choose a spanning tree T and root r. Put a vertex v in A or B according as d_T(r,v) is even or odd. If an edge uv had endpoints of the same parity, the unique u-v path in T would have even length, because its length is d_T(r,u)+d_T(r,v)-2d_T(r,w), with w the last common vertex of the root paths. The edge uv is not then a tree edge, and adjoining it to that simple tree path gives an odd cycle, a contradiction. Thus all edges cross A,B.

links.statement: No odd cycle implies a bipartition by spanning-tree depth parity.

glossary.G: the finite undirected graph in the theorem
glossary.A: one vertex class in a bipartition
glossary.B: the other vertex class in a bipartition
glossary.T: a spanning tree of a connected component of G
glossary.r: a chosen root vertex of T
glossary.d_T(r,v): the number of edges on the unique path in T from r to v
glossary.u: one endpoint of a considered edge of G
glossary.v: the other endpoint of a considered edge of G
glossary.w: the last common vertex of the root-to-u and root-to-v paths in T
